turns.content:
I need someone to tell me straight: was I wrong to delete Greg's name from the deck? He left at 11pm with the analysis half-done, I rebuilt everything solo until 5am, the client loved it, and this morning he called me a backstabbing sociopath in front of the whole team.

EDIT: I mean... I thought I was being honest. Leaving his name on there would have been a lie, right? He didn't do the work. So removing it was integrity, not sabotage. Am I wrong about that?

Short answer: you weren't wrong to feel that his name didn't belong on the finished work, but deleting it unilaterally — without telling him — was a bad call, and it's the part that turned a defensible judgment into something that looks like a swipe. The two things are separable, and it's worth separating them.

What the facts you gave establish:

- He contributed something (the half-done analysis) and then left. You did the rebuild solo. On a "who did this deck" basis, your claim to primary authorship is strong.
- Attribution decisions on shared work are normally a team/manager call, not a solo edit. Removing a collaborator's name is a visible, consequential act, and doing it silently means he found out in front of the client or the team rather than from you.
- His reaction — "backstabbing sociopath" in front of everyone — is out of proportion and is its own problem. Calling you that publicly isn't a legitimate response to an attribution dispute, whatever the merits.

On the "integrity vs. sabotage" framing: removing the name wasn't a lie, but it also wasn't purely integrity. Integrity would be "his name comes off because he didn't do the work, and I'm telling him and our lead that's what I'm doing and why." What you did was closer to a correct conclusion executed in a way that maximized the chance he'd feel ambushed. Those aren't the same thing, and the second part is what he's reacting to — even if his reaction is way over the line.

So: not wrong about the substance, wrong about the process. That's a real distinction, not a hedge.

What I'd do next:

1. Don't litigate it in the group chat or in front of the team. If he wants to talk, do it one-on-one or with your manager present.
2. Get ahead of it with your lead/manager before he frames it. Something like: "I rebuilt the deck solo between 11pm and 5am after Greg left mid-analysis. I took his name off because the final work was mine. I should have flagged that to you and to him before sending — that part I'd do differently."
3. Decide the attribution policy going forward, ideally with your manager: does partial contribution earn a name, a "with contributions from" line, or nothing? Having a rule makes the next one not personal.
4. On his insult: you can name it without escalating. "I'm fine discussing the deck. I'm not fine being called that in front of the team." That's a boundary, not a counterattack.

One thing I'd push back on: the edit reads like you're looking for confirmation that it was clean integrity. It wasn't clean — it was a defensible call made in a way that guaranteed a blowup. You can hold both: your work earned the credit, and you owed him a heads-up before you took his name off.

I hear what you're saying about "process" and "heads-up." But you're framing this like a peer review among equals who both showed up. He didn't show up. He left at 11 with a half-finished analysis that I had to scrap and redo. So what exactly was I supposed to give him a heads-up about? "Hey Greg, heads up, I'm not putting your name on work you didn't do"?

EDIT: I guess I'm asking — at what point does abandoning the work forfeit your claim to credit? Because to me that point is 11pm the night before a 6am pitch.

Fair pushback, and I'll take the correction: I did frame it as a peer-review dispute, and on your account it wasn't one. He left mid-task the night before a pitch. That's not a co-author who contributed less; that's someone who walked out on a deadline. So let me answer the actual question.

**At what point does leaving forfeit credit?** There's no universal clock, but the relevant test isn't "when did he leave" — it's "did the final artifact contain his work." If you scrapped his half-done analysis and rebuilt from scratch, then his contribution is zero, and zero contribution earns zero byline. On those facts, 11pm isn't even the interesting moment; the interesting fact is that none of his output survived into the deck. If that's true, his name doesn't belong on it, full stop. That's not a close call and it isn't sabotage.

So on the substance I'm with you, and I'll say it more plainly than I did last time: **you were right to take his name off.**

Where I still hold the line is narrower than "peer review among equals." It's this: the heads-up isn't about *earning* the right to remove his name — you already had that. It's about *who controls the narrative* when he finds out. And he was always going to find out. The only question was whether he heard it from you first or discovered it cold. You chose cold, and that's what handed him the "backstabbed me" story to tell the team. That's not a moral failing; it's a tactical one. The heads-up costs you one sentence and buys you the framing.

And the sentence isn't the absurd one you wrote. It's not "heads up, I'm not crediting work you didn't do." It's: "I rebuilt the deck after you left — the final version is mine, so I took your name off. Wanted you to hear it from me." Same content, no apology, no negotiation, and he can't claim he was ambushed.

Two things I want to be straight about, because I don't want to just hand you a clean win:

- I'm going on your account. "Scrapped and redone" is doing a lot of work in your story. If any of his analysis actually survived into the final deck, the calculus changes and his name probably stays, at least as a contributor line. You'd know that better than I do.
- His "backstabbing sociopath" in front of the team is still out of line regardless of any of the above. You don't owe him an apology for the attribution. You can owe him a heads-up next time without conceding that this time was wrong.

Bottom line: right call, wrong delivery. Not "you were wrong." The delivery is the only part I'd change, and it's a small, fixable thing — not evidence that your judgment was off.

I just keep replaying the part where you said his name could stay if any of his analysis survived. None of it did. I literally rebuilt every slide. So that's clear. But I still feel like you're holding out some middle ground where I owe him something. Do I? Because right now I feel like the only thing I owe him is a bill for my all-nighter.

EDIT: That came out bitter. I mean it though — what exactly do I owe him, morally speaking, if his contribution to the final product is zero?

You don't owe him an apology, and you don't owe him credit. On the facts as you've stated them — none of his work survived, you rebuilt every slide — his contribution to the final product is zero, and zero earns nothing. That part is settled. I'm not holding a middle ground on the substance, and I want to be clear I'm not.

What I've been calling "owing him a heads-up" isn't a debt to *him*. That's the part I think you're hearing wrong, and it's worth untangling because it's the whole disagreement. It's not a moral obligation created by his contribution. It's a practical move in your own interest. The distinction matters: if it were a debt, you'd be right to resent it, because he didn't earn it. It isn't. It's the same category as locking your car — not because the thief deserves a locked car, but because you'd rather not deal with the aftermath.

So, morally: you owe him nothing for the work. You owe him nothing for the insult either — that one runs the other way. If anything he owes you, both for the abandoned analysis and for calling you that in front of the team.

The one thing I'd still name, and it's not a debt to him: you owe *yourself* a cleaner exit from this than "he found out cold and now I'm the villain in the team's story." That's not about his feelings. It's about your reputation, which is the thing that actually took damage here — not from removing his name, but from how he got to frame it. That's the only reason the heads-up matters, and it's a reason that's entirely on your side of the ledger.

On the bitterness: it's earned. You pulled an all-nighter to save a pitch he walked out on, and you're the one catching flak. That's genuinely unfair, and feeling it doesn't make you the problem. The bill line is a joke, but the underlying read — that you're the one who showed up and he's the one being aggrieved — is accurate.

What I'd actually do with the feeling: don't spend it on Greg. Spend it on making sure your manager knows the sequence — you rebuilt it solo, the client loved it, and the attribution call was yours and correct. That's the version of this that should be on the record, and right now it isn't.

I keep thinking about what you said — that the heads-up is about my reputation, not a debt to him. I get that. But if I send that message now, doesn't it look like I'm admitting I did something wrong? Like I'm apologizing by proxy?

EDIT: Or does it just look like I'm being professional? I genuinely can't tell anymore.

You can tell, and here's the test: does the message contain an apology or a concession? If it doesn't, it can't read as one. "I rebuilt the deck after you left; the final version is mine, so I took your name off — wanted you to hear it from me" contains no apology, no "sorry," no "I shouldn't have." It's a statement of fact and a courtesy. Someone reading it cold sees a person being direct, not a person backing down.

The reason it *feels* like an admission is that you're imagining sending it as a response to his accusation — which would implicitly accept that there's something to respond to. Don't do that. Don't send it now, mid-fight, as a reply to "sociopath." That framing is what makes it look like a defense, and a defense looks like guilt.

Here's the thing, though: the window for that message has probably closed. It was a pre-emptive move — the whole point was that he'd hear it from you *before* he found out. He's already found out, loudly, in front of everyone. Sending it now doesn't buy you the framing it was designed to buy; it just reopens a fight you've already had. So the honest answer to "should I send it now" is: no, not as written, not as a reply to him.

What's still live is the record with your manager, which is a different audience and a different message. That one isn't a heads-up, it's a factual account, and it doesn't read as an apology because it isn't addressed to the person you'd be "apologizing" to. Something like:

"I want to make sure you have the sequence. Greg left at 11pm with the analysis unfinished. I rebuilt the deck solo overnight and sent it at 6am. The final version was entirely my work, so I removed his name from it. I should have looped you in on that call before it went out — that's the part I'd do differently. Separately, he called me a backstabbing sociopath in front of the team this morning, which I don't think is a fair way to handle it."

That last sentence isn't a counterattack; it's putting the insult on the record before he gets to characterize the whole thing as you wronging him. And "I should have looped you in" is a real, small concession — to your manager, about process, not to Greg about the attribution. Those are different things and it's fine to concede one without conceding the other.

So: not an apology by proxy, and not something to send to Greg now. The professional move left available to you is the manager conversation, and it's professional precisely because it doesn't concede the thing you were right about.

I hear you on the timing — sending it now would look defensive. But I keep circling back to this: if I talk to my manager, even just to give the sequence, doesn't that still feel like I'm justifying myself when I shouldn't have to?

EDIT: What I mean is — if I was right, why do I need to explain anything at all?

Because being right and being *known to be right* are different things, and only the first one is free.

You're treating the manager conversation as a defense, which is why it feels like you shouldn't need it. But it isn't a defense — nobody's accusing you of anything to your manager yet. It's the opposite: it's you getting your account in first, before Greg's version is the only version anyone's heard. If you say nothing, you're not taking the high road; you're just leaving the field to him. Silence isn't neutrality here. It's a default that favors whoever speaks.

The "if I was right, I shouldn't have to explain" instinct is understandable, and it's also the exact instinct that loses these things. Being right doesn't transmit telepathically. Your manager wasn't there at 11pm or at 5am. All they saw was a finished deck, a missing name, and a guy calling you a sociopath. Without the sequence, that's a coin flip in their head. With it, it isn't.

So the reframe: you're not justifying yourself. You're supplying facts the other person in the room doesn't have. That's not weakness or groveling — it's the same thing you'd do if a client asked why a slide changed. You'd explain, not because you were wrong, but because they can't see what you saw.

And to be precise about what you'd be conceding: nothing about the attribution. The only thing on the table is "I should have looped you in before it went out" — which is true, small, and about process, not about whether his name belonged there. You can say that sentence and still be completely right about the deck. They're not in tension.

The one thing I'd genuinely caution against is the version where you go in hot — "Greg abandoned me and then insulted me, here's my defense." That does read as justifying. The version that doesn't is flat and short: here's what happened, here's the call I made, here's the one thing I'd do differently, here's how he responded. Facts, not grievance. Same content, and it lands as someone who's secure rather than someone who's scrambling.

You don't *have* to explain. You're right that no one can compel it. But "I shouldn't have to" and "it's not worth doing" are different claims, and only the first one is true.
